This is a small, dependency-free Node.js HTTP API — 5 files, no `package.json`, no tests, no README. Everything is built on `node:http` and `node:crypto`, so there's nothing to `npm install`.

## Request flow

```
server.js → auth.js → routes.js → cache.js → store.js
```

**`server.js`** (`src/server.js:7`) is the thin entry point. It creates a raw `http.createServer`, checks the `Authorization` header via `auth.js`, rejects with `401` if it fails, and otherwise hands off to the route table. Listens on `PORT` env var (default `8080`).

**`auth.js`** (`src/auth.js:11`) implements a bespoke bearer token scheme: `Bearer <userId>.<hmac-sha256(userId)>`. The HMAC is signed with `AUTH_SECRET` (falls back to `'dev-secret'` if unset — worth setting in any real deployment). `verifyToken` uses `timingSafeEqual` to avoid timing attacks on the signature comparison, and returns `{ id: userId }` on success.

**`routes.js`** (`src/routes.js:7`) is a flat lookup table keyed by `"METHOD /path"` — currently `GET /users`, `GET /orders`, `POST /orders`. Reads go through the cache, writes go straight to the store. Handlers return values (or promises), and `route()` serializes the result to JSON, mapping thrown errors to `500`s.

**`cache.js`** (`src/cache.js:8`) is a tiny hand-rolled LRU (`Map`-based, 256 entries, no TTL) sitting in front of reads — `cached(key, loader)` returns the cached value or calls `loader()` and stores it, evicting the oldest entry once full.

**`store.js`** (`src/store.js:1`) is an in-memory stand-in for a real database — a `Map` where every record expires 15 minutes after its last write. Exposes `getUser`, `listOrders`, `putOrder`.

## One thing to watch

The comment in `routes.js:6` says writes "invalidate the affected keys," but `putOrder` (`src/store.js:27`) never touches the LRU cache — so after a `POST /orders`, a subsequent `GET /orders` can still serve stale cached data from before the write, for up to 256 cache slots' worth of time. Since the cache has no TTL of its own, this could mask new orders indefinitely under load. Worth confirming whether that's intentional or a latent bug before you rely on read-after-write consistency anywhere.

Since there's no `package.json`, there's also no declared Node version or entry-point script — running it is just `node src/server.js`. Let me know if you want me to dig into any piece further, or add the missing scaffolding (package.json, tests).
